analysis.one_liner: Protects workers' traditional pensions when employers convert them to cash balance plans.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor action in the Senate and died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: In the early 2000s, many large employers converted traditional pensions (defined benefit plans) into 'cash balance' plans, a change that often slowed or stopped the growth of benefits for mid-career and older workers. This bill would have overridden proposed Treasury regulations that critics said allowed those conversions to reduce older workers' accruals, applied age discrimination law to cash balance conversions, and given workers age 40 or older (or with 10 years of service) both notice and the right, at retirement, to choose their benefits under the old plan formula or the new one. It also set a test for when a conversion at a large plan (100 or more participants) illegally 'wears away' benefits already earned.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in traditional defined benefit pension plans, especially those age 40 or older or with 10 or more years of service, whose benefit accruals were being reduced when employers converted plans to cash balance or similar hybrid formulas. The bill would have guaranteed them notice, a side-by-side comparison of what the change costs them, and an election at retirement to receive benefits under the pre-conversion formula, and would have protected early retirement subsidies they had qualified for.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Older and long-tenured pension plan participants

how_it_helps.text: Requires employers, when a conversion amendment takes effect, to give workers who are 40 or older or have 10 years of service a notice comparing their projected benefit with and without the change [S2, S3].

Gives those workers an election at retirement to receive benefits either under the plan in effect at retirement or under the plan in effect immediately before the conversion, including accrued early retirement subsidies [S2, S3].

Directs that ERISA, the tax code, and the Age Discrimination in Employment Act be applied without regard to the Treasury's December 2002 proposed regulations on age-based reductions of accruals and cross-testing in cash balance plans [S2, S3].

Sets a formula under which a conversion adopted by a plan with 100 or more participants is treated as reducing accrued benefits if the participant's benefit could at any time fall below what the old and new formulas combined would have produced [S2, S3].
Applies retroactively to plan amendments adopted before enactment, unless the IRS had already issued a determination letter approving the amendment before April 8, 2003 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that sponsor defined benefit pension plans, especially large ones that had converted or wanted to convert to cash balance designs. They would bear notice and administrative costs and would lose the ability to reduce older workers' future accruals through conversions, which was the main cost saving those conversions produced.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes compliance costs on plan sponsors: notices comparing benefits with and without the amendment, election tracking at retirement, and administration of the anti-wear-away test [S2, S3].

Its retroactive application to amendments already in effect (except IRS-approved ones) would have created legal uncertainty for employers that had already completed conversions, and the strongest good-faith objection is that by raising the cost of converting plans it could push employers to freeze or terminate defined benefit plans entirely rather than maintain them under the new restrictions [S3].
The protections apply only to participants age 40 or older or with 10 years of service, leaving younger, shorter-tenured workers without an election when a plan converts [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the workers covered, the benefit was concrete: their earned pensions and early retirement subsidies could not be quietly eroded by a formula change, and they would see the comparison themselves. The costs fall on plan sponsors as compliance burden and lost flexibility, and the retroactive reach was aggressive, which is the fair criticism of the design. The bill did nothing for workers in defined contribution (401(k)-type) plans, and its age-and-service cutoffs leave out newer employees, but for its intended beneficiaries the protections outweigh the administrative costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Harkin introduced the Pension Benefits Protection Act of 2003 on April 8, 2003, with Senators Durbin, Feingold, Kennedy, and Boxer as original cosponsors [S1, S3].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day of introduction [S1, S5].
Six Democratic senators cosponsored the bill; no Republican did [S4].
The action history shows no hearings, no committee markup, no floor vote, and no further action of any kind after the referral [S5].
The 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, and the bill died in committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that had converted pension plans to cash balance designs, or planned to, were better off because the bill died: the Treasury regulations the bill would have overridden and the accrual reductions at issue faced no legislative obstacle, and older workers' converted pensions received no new protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers that converted pensions to cash balance plans

for.name: Sen. Tom Harkin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup and never reported the bill; the record shows no action after the referral.

against.name: Large employers converting to cash balance pension plans
against.role: Plan sponsors affected by the bill
against.what_they_did: Opposed legislative restrictions on cash balance conversions during this period, favoring the Treasury's proposed regulations the bill would have overridden.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all six cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-run Senate committee took no action; there is no record of Republican support for the bill.

industries.industry: Large employers sponsoring defined benefit pension plans
industries.note: The bill would have barred these employers from using cash balance and similar conversions to cut older workers' future accruals and would have required notice and a benefit election for covered employees, eliminating a major cost-saving mechanism. Its interest in stopping the bill ran directly against the workers whose pensions were at stake.

industries.industry: Employee benefits law and consulting firms
industries.note: New notice, election, and anti-wear-away compliance requirements would have generated work for benefits consultants and actuaries, while the ban on the proposed Treasury regulations would have upended the advice being given on cash balance conversions.
